triage_digest.tier_profile: 6 T1 / 18 T2 / 8 T3 / 2 T4 — strong Tier-1 backbone (CSA, Georgia Tech, MCP spec, Google)
signal: Senior experience gradient is the defining finding: 81% productivity gain for 10+yr devs vs zero measurable improvement for juniors [claim-003, T2, 2 convergent sources]. This is the only finding that splits cleanly by audience — ideal for targeting.

Security debt is quantified and Tier-1 sourced: 45% OWASP Top 10 in AI code [claim-004, T1, Veracode], AI-attributed CVEs grew 6x in 90 days [claim-004, T1, Georgia Tech]. High-stakes enough to drive action.
Adoption is table-stakes: 77-92% daily use [claim-001, T2, 3 sources]. No longer a novelty angle — sets the frame but cannot be the spine.

Anthropic contradiction: internal study shows 'no significant speedup' when accounting for prompt time [con-001], directly challenging 10x vendor claims. Resolution depends on task clarity and experience level.
noise_and_thin_ice: N1 [temporal risk]: Claim-005 (Claude Code overtook Copilot) rests on Zylos T2 and a T3 GitHub comparison — usage rankings shift monthly; cannot be load-bearing.
N2 [vendor bias]: Claim-009 (three camps taxonomy) includes a T4 Windsurf vendor comparison as its largest source. The category split is real; the specific product rankings are not durable.
N3 [measurement gap]: Market size claims (claim-002: $11.7B) lack disclosed methodology and may include adjacent categories. Use as background only.
N4 [self-report bias]: 81% senior productivity gain (claim-003) is survey-based; no RCT backs this specific figure. Anthropic's RCT data (contradiction) suggests the real effect is task-dependent.
N5 [correlation trap]: 58% expect smaller teams (claim-007) — this is expectation data, not observed outcome. Do not frame as prediction.
N6 [gap severity]: SWE-bench data was inaccessible (403). Cannot provide benchmark evidence for agent comparison claims.
triage_digest.dedup_note: 12 duplicate claims merged. Key statistics (adoption %, OWASP 45%, CVE growth) converge independently across sources — safe to lead with.
triage_digest.followup_rationale: Gaps are framing constraints (benchmark data, longitudinal studies) that the article can disclose rather than chase. The contradiction (Anthropic vs vendor claims) is resolved by experience-level framing and encoded as a counterpoint section.

chosen_angle.working_h1: The Experience Divide: Why AI Coding Tools Deliver 81% Gains to Senior Developers and Zero to Juniors
chosen_angle.alt_h1: AI Coding Assistants: The 81% Gap Between Senior and Junior Productivity
chosen_angle.thesis: AI coding assistants have become table-stakes infrastructure, but their productivity payoff is not distributed evenly — it concentrates in hands that already know what good code looks like. Senior developers (10+ years) report 81% gains while juniors show zero measurable improvement, because the value of these tools scales with the ability to review, redirect, and catch what the model misses. The same forces that make AI powerful for experts make it dangerous for the rest: 45% of AI-generated code carries OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities, and AI-attributed CVEs grew sixfold in three months.
chosen_angle.audience: Senior/staff software engineers (8+ years) evaluating AI tooling strategy; secondarily engineering leaders setting team adoption policy.
chosen_angle.rationale: Highest composite score on search intent (this audience is actively researching whether AI tools help them specifically), novelty (the senior/junior divide is the most differentiated finding in the corpus — not widely framed this way), and taxonomy alignment (fits a senior-dev-focused publication or newsletter). The 81%/0% split provides immediate narrative tension and lets every section ladder back to the experience variable.

blueprint.tone: authoritative, data-driven, peer-to-peer; speak as a senior engineer to senior engineers; allow one measured line of wit per section; zero hype, zero doom; every stat carries an inline source tag

blueprint.argument_progression: Hook with the 81%/0% paradox -> frame adoption as universal but outcomes as bifurcated -> explain WHY experience matters (review capability, failure library, task clarity) -> quantify the cost of unreviewed AI code (security, duplication) -> steelman the optimists (where juniors and tooling genuinely help) -> synthesize the role shift -> close with a practical protocol + forward-looking disclosure box

avoid_claims: Do NOT present 81% senior gain as settled fact — it's T2 self-reported data; Anthropic RCT (con-001) shows it's task-dependent.
Do NOT state CVE growth as a confirmed rate — true count is 5-10x higher than confirmed (per Georgia Tech gap note).
Do NOT rank specific tools (Cursor vs Claude Code vs Copilot) as factual — Tier-2/3 sources, fast decay; use categories only.
Do NOT claim juniors are hurt by AI — no RCT data; present as unknown [H].
Do NOT frame '58% expect smaller teams' as a prediction — it's expectation survey data.
Do NOT cite market size ($11.7B) as precise — methodology undisclosed in source.
Do NOT reuse any dossier source URL in final citations — verify against originals (especially claim-004 chains).
Do NOT exceed 2 sentences on MCP/ACP — Tier-1 fact but not central to the experience divide angle.
Do NOT present the Anthropic contradiction as resolved — it is framework-dependent, not settled.
Do NOT use 'AI coding assistants' phrase in H2 titles (keep headings human-readable).
writer_contract.style: Authoritative, peer-to-peer, evidence-first. One measured line of wit per section max. No hype, no doom. Every stat gets inline source. [H] and [X] labels MUST survive to publication as explicit hedging. ~2,200 words +/-10%.
